_note: The public what's-new feed, rendered at the bottom of the Methodology page. Committed rather than built: web/data/ is generated and gitignored, and this is a written record, not an output. NEWEST FIRST. `kind` is one of ship (a feature), model (the numbers changed), fix (something was wrong), or refuse (something was measured and deliberately not built) — the last one matters as much as the first three, because a decision nobody wrote down gets re-made by somebody who has not seen the reasoning. A `model` entry must name what moved on the board; see engine/ledger.MODEL_ERAS, which the same page renders beside these with the results each era actually produced.

entries.title: Grading picks takes the server a fraction of the time
entries.body: The pass that grades finished picks read each day's box scores once for every open pick, checked every pick ever graded for corrected stats, and rewrote the whole Record page, every five minutes; its first timed run took over eighteen minutes. It now reads each day once, checks the last week (every night it still checks them all), and updates the Record page every ten minutes. No grade changes.

entries.title: Busy game days leave more of the server for the boards
entries.body: Every few minutes the server grades the picks whose games have finished, and on a game day it was also refitting six of its learning models on nearly every one of those passes, close to ten minutes of work every five. Picks still grade the moment their games end; the learning models now refit at most once an hour, and never skip a graded pick.

entries.title: The weather desk measures how sure it should be
entries.body: The weather desk is still paused. Its forecasts were right about the day but too sure about the degree: it priced every city's high as if the forecast were rarely more than two degrees off. It now measures that from its own record, each forecast it logged beside the bracket that actually won that day, and grades the calls it would make with the measured spread, out of sight, until they win about what they claim.

entries.title: The Lab's football replay fits inside its nightly hour
entries.body: The Lab's NFL numbers have been dated 29 September because the replay ran past the hour the server gives it and published nothing. It now reads its closing lines once, inside its own half hour, and starts a week only when there is time to finish it, so the NFL section is written before the hour is up.

entries.title: Leagues out of season stop rebuilding every few minutes
entries.body: Baseball's page was being rebuilt every few minutes for a slate with no games, about three minutes of the server's time out of every twenty. A league whose season is over now refreshes every six hours, and that time goes to the leagues being played and to the models' weekly refit.

entries.title: The nightly jobs run once a day, as they should
entries.body: Two of the server's background routines kept their notes in one file and could overwrite each other's, so a job that had already run that day was sometimes started again: on 7 November the model refit ran four times. Each now records only its own notes, so the nightly jobs run once and the boards keep the server to themselves for the rest of the day.

entries.title: The weekly model refit gets its share of the server
entries.body: The models' weekly refit and the weekly backtests were running at the very lowest priority on the server, behind every board rebuild, so they got about an eighth of the processor and every large fit was cut off at its time limit: the NFL's recency weights still dated from August, and the backtests had not replayed the NFL since 29 September. They were meant to run level with the board rebuilds, and now they do, with the site itself still first in line.

entries.title: The weekly model refit no longer spends nights on finished seasons
entries.body: The models re-learn each sport from its whole history a piece at a time, a little each night. On 7 November baseball and the WNBA, their seasons over, held two of the round's places while the NFL's recency weights still dated from August. A league whose season is over, with its next one more than three weeks away, now sits the round out, and the weekly backtests stop replaying it once its last games are in. It comes back three weeks before its season, so its models are fitted on everything it played before the first game is priced.

entries.title: Leagues out of season are greyed in the league row
entries.body: A league whose season is over now shows grey in the row of leagues at the top of the page, so the ones playing tonight stand out: today that is baseball and the WNBA. It is still a button and its page still opens, with everything on it; hovering over it says the season is over. A league turns grey when the season calendar says it is done, or sooner when its own scoreboard shows the last game of the postseason has been played (the same signal that stops the site buying odds for it), and turns back the day its season starts.

entries.title: Every closing line is the player's own
entries.body: A closing line is the number a bet is measured against at kickoff, and the record's closing-line value is built from them. Early in the season the odds feed could file one player's prices under another's name when the two shared a first initial and a surname and the second man's own prices were missing from that pull: Amon-Ra St. Brown's Week 1 receiving numbers were also filed under A.J. Brown, four days after A.J. Brown had played the season's opener. No close reads such a copy now, a close that came from one is read again from the player's own prices or left empty when he has none, and the feed only fills a missing price from a game it can prove is the player's. Grades and results are unchanged; only closing-line value moves, for the bets it touched.

entries.title: The models' weekly refit finishes what it starts
entries.body: The weekly refit re-learns each sport from its whole history, a piece at a time, a little each night. Last night four long jobs shared the server's one processor at once, and the refit ran out its time inside the NFL's first fit without finishing a market, though on its own that fit takes about five minutes. Two of those jobs, the refit and the Lab's replay, now take turns. A week's round of refits also used to start over every Wednesday and throw away what it had finished, so the NFL, whose turn comes about once a week, never got through; a round now runs to its end before the next begins, and a fit that makes no progress in two full runs is set aside so the rest of the sport still refits. Nothing on the board moves until those refits land.

entries.title: A back's carries go up in the rain
entries.body: Measured on ten NFL seasons: in rain, teams run more (their running backs' carries were 6.9% higher than usual, in nine seasons of ten), and a back keeps his share of them. So a back's carries now rise when rain is forecast, by the forecast's own chance: a 70% chance of rain is 70% of the step. His rushing yards stay where they were, because per carry backs gained less in rain in most seasons, so the extra carries do not reliably add yards; the card says so. College reads the same table. And a team on an inexperienced quarterback ran about 5% more, but mostly on the quarterback's own runs; the lead back's numbers barely moved, so his card says that and his projection does not change.

entries.title: Kalshi's spreads and totals on hockey and basketball games
entries.body: The game page's market section now carries Kalshi's price on the NHL's puck line and total, and on the NBA's spread and total, beside Polymarket's: the chance the crowd gives the home side to cover the board's own line, and the over on the board's own total. Only the same bet the books quote counts, never a neighbouring line. Kalshi lists both leagues' markets in the same shape as football's, which the box confirmed before they were wired in.

entries.title: The models' weekly refit no longer waits on a piece it cannot finish
entries.body: The weekly refit re-learns each sport from its whole history in pieces, a few each morning. One of the NBA's checks was started with too little time left and cut off every run, and the NBA's own fits waited on it all week. Each piece now starts only with its own time left, and a piece that runs the most a run can give without finishing is set aside for the week, keeping its last result, so the rest goes ahead.

entries.title: The Lab opens to free accounts
entries.body: A free account can now open the Lab and see how well each sport's model forecast games it never saw: how many props the replay priced, the Brier score, the skill over guessing the base rate and the calibration error, sport by sport. The replay market by market, with the bets it would have made at the price and their grades, stays with a membership. About, Methodology, Status, Why Us, Features and Alerts were already open to free accounts; the Lab was the last of the seven. The Terms' list of free features names it.

entries.title: The Lab's replay fits its night again
entries.body: The Lab replays each model over the games it has stored and publishes how well it forecast them, one sport at a time. Its nightly run was being stopped at its hour inside the first sport, so the page stayed dated 29 September. The run now has a time limit of its own: a sport starts only while there is time to finish it, the NBA and WNBA stop between markets at the pace the last one took, and a market not reached keeps last week's numbers, dated. The sports left over go first the next night, so each sport's numbers come back within a few nights and stay within a week after that.

entries.title: Rocket Radar's record follows every call
entries.body: The radar's record called a coin gone the moment it left the 60 coins we scan, and new pools push the older ones out within minutes. So nearly every call read gone while its coin was still trading, and only the coins still trending got their 6-hour and later checks: a record of survivors. Every call is now priced at 1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours and a week by its own lookup, on our scan or off it; a check counts only when it is taken on time; and gone means no pool was quoting the coin when we looked. The record counts calls from 6 November. The calls before it are kept, and the page says why they are not in its numbers.

entries.title: College props are corrected on the model's own number
entries.body: Each week we measure how far every market's probabilities run hot or cold and correct them. For college football, and for the NFL's recency and player-memory settings, that measurement was taken on probabilities already pulled toward the betting line, while the board applies the correction before that pull. Replayed on four NFL seasons, learned on 2022-24 and judged on 2025, the correction learned on the model's own number beat the old one on all four markets, and the old one did worse than no correction at all on three. From each sport's next weekly refit, college's corrections and the NFL's and college's recency and player-memory settings are learned the right way. Where the old correction was stretching college's probabilities, its edges will come out smaller. The NFL's yardage and catch markets keep their corrections learned against real sportsbook lines.

entries.title: The weekly refit runs faster and keeps its place
entries.body: Our weekly refit, which re-learns each sport from its whole history, had not finished the NFL since late August: its recency step ran past the hour on our server and lost all four markets' work each time. Each fit now reads the model's settings once rather than on every game it replays, with the same numbers to the last digit, and the recency step keeps each market the moment it is fitted, so a run that runs out of time picks up at the next market. The board prices props a little faster for the same reason, and each NFL board build reads the league's defensive-coverage file once instead of once for every opponent.

entries.title: The site keeps its own record of what breaks inside it
entries.body: When something broke on our server, the only trace was a line in the server's system log, which our daily bug scan cannot read. The site now writes its own note: the kind of error and where in our code it happened, with anything a reader typed taken out, and never an address, an account or a page. The bug scan reads it, and the owner's desk counts the day's errors and shows the commonest. The Privacy Policy says so in its section on crash reports.

entries.title: The owner's desk shows the weekly jobs
entries.body: The deep refit, the Lab's replay, board learning and the backups each run once a week beside the boards, and what each did could only be read off the server. The owner's desk now has a card for them: each one's last run, how long it took, whether its hour ran out and the last thing it said; how far the refit's round has got and what it still owes; and the date each sport's Lab numbers are from, in amber when they are late.

entries.title: The Lab's baseball replay fits its weekly run
entries.body: The Lab replays the model over stored history once a week, and its baseball replay walked every stored season for three markets, which on its own outran the run's hour, so baseball could not publish. It now walks the latest two seasons, which is what the page is about, and stops between markets when the time runs short. A market it didn't reach keeps last week's numbers, marked with the date they were replayed, and the page names the seasons it covers.

entries.title: The owner's desk lists the commands waiting on the server
entries.body: Every command waiting to be run on the site's server is written down in one file, in the order to run it, and reading that file meant opening it somewhere else on a phone. The owner's desk now has a card for it: each step folded under its heading, each command with a Copy button, so nothing gets typed by hand. It reads the same file the site was built from, so it changes when the list does.

entries.title: NHL saves: the right level and the right spread
entries.body: We replayed every start of two NHL seasons through the saves model. It projected 5–6% more saves than goalies made, because a starter does not face every shot his team allows: some nights he is pulled, and the empty net takes the rest. It was also about 22% too sure of itself, so the misses landed wider than it said. Both are fixed, and the night after a team played moves the shots a goalie faces: more against a tired team, fewer from one. Measured on the season each fix never saw, the saves chances got better by more than any other change in the NHL lab. Every saves card now reads from the corrected model.

entries.title: WNBA: three minutes pieces measured on the WNBA's own six seasons
entries.body: The WNBA board runs the NBA's code with its own settings, and the NBA's measured minutes pieces were switched off for it until WNBA games said so. We replayed six WNBA regular seasons (2021 to 2026) through the board's own projection. Three pieces made minutes and points better in every one of the six. The first is the starting five's news: before the tip, who of a club's last starting five is ruled out, who is back, and each player's own starts. The second is a player's first game back after missing games. The third weights his newest games more heavily. Together they cut the minutes error by about 3% in every season. The role jump, the second game back and a regular's return each made points worse in at least one season, so they stay off for the WNBA. The board plays again in May.

entries.title: Hockey's games get the prediction markets' price
entries.body: Every game page shows the win chance at each prediction market beside the sportsbooks, and every build records it before the game. Hockey asked both markets for its games and never got an answer, because neither reader listed the NHL. Both do now, so an NHL game page shows Polymarket's and Kalshi's price when they list the game. The pregame record that measures whether the crowd knows more than the books starts counting hockey games too.

entries.title: NHL: the model measured on three seasons, and back-to-backs priced on both sides
entries.body: Every NHL setting had been a first guess. We replayed three full seasons of NHL box scores through the board's own model, each setting chosen on one season and judged on the other, and changed only what held up both ways. A skater's scoring rate now reads a longer stretch of his games, and his ice time a shorter one: every prop market got better on the season the fit never saw. A team's strength is believed more slowly, and moneyline, puck line and totals all improved in both seasons. Back-to-backs now count on both sides: a team on its second night scores about 7% fewer goals than the model expected, and its rested opponent about 4% more. The old adjustment covered only the tired side, at 3%. Each skater's number moves with it, by three-quarters of what two seasons measured: fewer shots and goals for the tired side, more against it. His card says so. When the probable goalie started last night, he starts again only 9% of the time. The card now names the goalie who usually takes that night, who starts 78% of the time, and still no saves bet rides on him.

entries.title: The owner's desk: who stays, the emails, a morning summary and spreadsheets
entries.body: Four more things on the owner's desk. Who stays: each week's new accounts, how many came back after their first day, how many were here this past week and how many pay, with what a paying member brings in a month, how many paid plans were cancelled and what a paying member is worth over a membership. The emails: every email the site sends is now counted by the part of the site that sent it and whether it went, never the address, and a day when more fail than go is sent to the owner's phones. A morning summary: yesterday in one line (accounts made, subscriptions started, paying members, the month's revenue, the picks' record) on the owner's phones after 8am, with a switch to turn it off. And four of the desk's tables download as spreadsheets. All of it is counts and the business's own numbers.

entries.title: The owner's desk sees the business, the backups and the sign-ins
entries.body: The owner's desk gained six things the server already kept but never showed. Each sport's books: picks journaled today and the last 7 and 30 days won-lost and units, with a warning when a league plays today and nothing has posted. The way to paying: visits, accounts made, plan buttons tapped and subscriptions started this month, and how many of the trials that have ended turned paying, with the business kept day by day from now on. How people use the site, from the usage counts the Privacy Policy describes in section 2.5. The odds credits each league spent today and this month. The backups: how old the newest nightly copy of each database is, whether it reached the offsite copy, and the weekly zip. And the security log as counts: sign-ins, failures, the rate limit and Stripe's signatures. A late backup, a missed offsite copy, fifty failed sign-ins in an hour or Stripe's messages failing their signature now go under Needs you and to the owner's phones. The account list can be filtered by where each account stands. All of it is counts and the business's own numbers; no one is named.

entries.title: The owner's desk lists every account
entries.body: The Accounts card on the owner's desk now lists every account, newest first, by its number: where its membership stands, when it joined and when it was last here. Who an account is shows only when the owner opens it, one account at a time, as the Privacy Policy has always said; its section 2.14 now describes the list as well.

entries.title: Closing lines come from the sportsbooks' number, not an exchange's ladder
entries.body: Every settled pick records the market's closing line, which is how the Record page measures whether a pick beat the close. Exchanges like Novig and ProphetX post a ladder of lines for a player where a sportsbook posts one, and the two places that read the close let those rungs in: one kept whichever quote was stored last, the other took the middle of every quote, rungs and all. On 1,062 of 2,537 settled NBA picks the recorded close was 3 or more away from the pick's own line; Zach Edey's rebounds at 9.5 and 10.5 'closed' at 19.5. The close is now each book's last quote before the game, at the sportsbooks' number, and an exchange's only when no sportsbook quoted. Grades and results never read it. Picks settled before today keep the close they were given until a repair pass re-reads them, which never touches a grade.

entries.title: On an iPhone, the tab bar stays at the bottom when a menu or the keyboard opens
entries.body: On an iPhone, the Home page's Sort menu opens a picker from the bottom of the screen, as the keyboard does, without making the page any shorter. The tab bar, pinned to the bottom of the screen, rode up with the picker and could stay halfway up the page after it closed, over the games. Now, while a picker or the keyboard is up, the tab bar and the bets-riding strip above it step aside, as an app's own bar does, and when it closes they come back at the bottom. Other phones keep their bar as before.

entries.title: NBA first basket: which team scores first, by the two players who jump
entries.body: A first-basket chance is the chance his team scores first times his share of it. The team half came from each team's record of taking the game's first shot, with a lean toward the home team. Replayed on two full seasons, it was worse than a coin flip at picking who shoots first. The home lean was too strong (home teams took the first shot about half the time), and a team's record changes with whoever jumps for it. We now keep every game's opening jump ball, and the board reads tonight's two jumpers: how often each one's side has won the tip, with a small home lean, and the team that wins the tip takes the first shot 88% of the time. With every setting chosen on the other season, it was clearly better than a coin and better than the old way in both seasons. Each pick's card names the jumper. Games played before today are read back a batch each night.

entries.title: NBA first basket: shared among tonight's likely starting five
entries.body: The first basket almost always goes to one of the five players on the floor at the tip. Our first-basket chances counted each player's shots in the first three minutes over the season, which mixes how often he starts with how much he shoots when he does. A new starter, or a starter back from injury, looked like a small chance, and a player moved to the bench kept a starter's. Stars were overstated: players we gave a 34% share scored 25% of their team's first baskets. The board now reads tonight's likely starting five before the tip: the team's last starting five without anyone ruled out, plus a starter coming back, filled to five. It shares the first basket among them by each player's opening shots per start. Replayed on two full seasons, with each season's settings chosen on the other, the chances were sharper in both (multi-class Brier 0.858 to 0.827 and 0.856 to 0.821) and match how often players actually scored first. Each pick's card says whether he is in tonight's likely five.

entries.title: NBA first basket: no chance for a player who is not playing
entries.body: Our first-basket picks give each player a share of his team's first basket from his shots in the first three minutes of its recent games. They never asked who plays tonight, so a player ruled out kept his share and every teammate who played was shorted. On two full seasons replayed, at least one such player was in the pool for 60% of teams' first baskets. Taking the players who did not play out of the pool made the chance on the actual first scorer 9-10% sharper overall, and 14-16% sharper in those games, in both seasons. The board now takes out everyone the injury report rules out before the chances are drawn, and a price on one of them is never a pick.

entries.title: Picks stay on the board until the game really starts
entries.body: The 7pm NBA games on 4 November tipped around 7:10. The site took their picks off the board at 7:00, by the printed time, while the Live tab, which follows the scoreboard, had nothing on those games until the ball went up. For those ten minutes the picks were on neither page, though the books were still taking bets on them. Now, for up to 45 minutes past a game's printed time, a scoreboard read from the last three minutes that still says the game has not started keeps its picks on the board, and they move to Live the moment it tips. If the scoreboard goes quiet, the printed time decides as before, so a pick is never held on the board through a game.

entries.title: NBA: who starts tonight moves his minutes
entries.body: About one NBA game in eleven, a player does the other thing from his last game: the bench man starts, or the starter comes off the bench. Those games carried a sixth of our minutes misses: a bench man who starts played 3.6 minutes over our number, a starter sent to the bench about 4 under. The starting five is only confirmed half an hour before the tip, but a good part of it is known earlier, and the board now reads it: the injury report on each club's last starting five (a bench man starts about a quarter of the time when one of them is ruled out), a regular coming back who started before he sat (the man who filled in usually goes back to the bench), and each player's own starts over his last ten. Fitted on one season and tested on the other, both ways, it took 1.3-1.7% off the minutes error over every priced game and 0.3% off points, and 2.3-3.4% off minutes in the games it moves. The card says when it moved a player. The box re-checks it every week on its own seasons and turns it off by itself if it ever stops paying.

entries.title: NBA: the chances on Most Likely's alternate lines say what they land
entries.body: Most Likely picks from each player's alternate lines (15+ points, 20+, 25+), well away from his main line. The correction the board learns from its own replays was measured only near the main line and then applied to every alternate line too, where it was the wrong size: on two seasons of replayed games, alternate lines it put at 72-86% landed about 90%, so fewer NBA picks cleared Most Likely's tiers than should have and the chances shown sold them short. The alternate lines now get their own correction, measured on alternate lines one and one and a half curve-widths either side of the projection. Fitted on half the games and tested on the other half, those chances land on what they say (PRA lines shown at 91% landed 91%), and every market's alternate lines price at least as well as before. The main line keeps its own correction. The weekly refit fits the new one; until it has, every line prices as it did.

entries.title: NFL: the teammate-out numbers come out the same on every computer
entries.body: When a teammate at his position is ruled out, the NFL board moves a player's number by a multiplier measured on four seasons. Re-running that measurement on a newer Python gave a slightly different answer (a running back's rushing behind a back just ruled out: 1.103 instead of the 1.102 that shipped), because Python 3.12 changed how it adds decimals and two games whose form landed exactly on the measurement's floor fell a hair under it and were dropped. The sums are exact now and a game on the floor counts, so the measurement gives one answer everywhere. The numbers that shipped were right. The version that ranks the depth chart by snap share, which the board uses when it has snap counts, had gone stale since Cincinnati's backs were added in October and was measured again: thirteen multipliers, none moving more than 0.006.

entries.title: NBA: rebounds, assists, steals, blocks and turnovers read past a player's last twenty games
entries.body: The NBA board read each player's rate a minute from his last twenty games only. For the rare stats that is a small sample (about fifteen steals for a guard), so one hot or cold fortnight moved his number as much as a real change. Now his older games (his last sixty, any club) and the league's rate for his role join the twenty's. On two full seasons of the league's own box scores, each judged on the one it never saw: steals 4.5% closer, turnovers 3.3%, blocks 2.7-4.0%, rebounds 2.0-3.2%, assists 1.6-2.4%, and the chances 0.5-1.5% better in every one of them on the board's own replay. A guard with no blocks in twenty games no longer has the under called a certainty. Points and threes stay as they were: read the same way they came out no better as chances. What moves: the projection, and so every pick, of every NBA rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers and rebounds-plus-assists prop, and the rebounds and assists inside points-plus-rebounds, points-plus-assists and PRA; the pick shows the step "Rate, read past his last twenty". The box checks it on its own seasons every week and turns it off if they disagree.

entries.title: NBA: when a regular sits, his minutes go to the bench, not the stars
entries.body: When a regular is ruled out, the board's teammate-out step hands his minutes to the rest of the rotation. It used to share them in proportion to each man's own minutes, so the stars took the most. Measured on two full seasons, each judged on the one it never saw, the minutes really go to the men with room to play more: the bench and the back of the rotation, while a star near his ceiling gains little. Shared that way, a teammate's minutes land 6-8% closer and his points 1-2% closer in those games than shared by minutes, and 10-12% and 3.5% closer than with no step at all. What moves: the projected minutes, and so every prop, of the teammates of a ruled-out regular; it switches on by itself once the server's own weekly check holds on its stored games.

entries.title: The NBA board switches on its own measured improvements
entries.body: Three NBA changes our lab measured on two full seasons were waiting for someone to run a check on the server: a spread that follows each player's projection (it fixes Most Likely calling picks 62% that have hit 66%), the minutes a sitting regular opens up for his teammates, and the rotation's rules for a player's first games back, a jump in his minutes and a regular's return. The server now runs all three checks itself every week, against the same bars, on its own stored games, right before the NBA's weekly refit. A change switches on only when its check passes, and the spread only after the refit has fitted its probabilities to it; a check that stops passing switches it back off.

entries.title: The NBA's own graded picks now grade the scout's warnings
entries.body: The six NBA warnings on the cards were measured on two seasons of box scores. From today the site also checks them against its own NBA picks, every few hours, the way it already does for the NFL and college: for each settled Most Likely pick it rebuilds the situation the pick was taken in (who sat, who came back, his rest and recent games, the game's spread and total) and compares how often picks carrying each warning hit with how often we said they would. A warning lowers a chance only once our own record proves, on games the check never saw, that picks carrying it come in under their claim; until then nothing moves. The Record page's "What it learned" shows each warning's record under the NBA once fifteen graded picks carry it. The NBA board also keeps each game's spread and total as it prices them now, so the shootout and blowout warnings can be graded from today on.

entries.title: NBA minutes read the rotation: a player's first games back, a minutes jump, a regular's return
entries.body: Minutes decide most of an NBA prop, and the board read a player's minutes only from his recent games. Three things it did not know, each measured on two full seasons before it moved a number (fitted on one season, judged on the other, kept only if minutes and points both landed closer in both): a player in his first game back plays fewer minutes than his old role, about 4% fewer after one missed game, 8% after two to four, 16% after five or more, and his second game back after a longer absence about 4% fewer; when his minutes have just jumped well above his usual, the jump mostly holds, so his projection moves most of the way there; and when a regular who has missed two or more games comes back, the players who covered for him give back about a quarter of his minutes. In the games they touch, minutes land 1% to 35% closer and points 0.5% to 8.6%. The pick says when one moved a player.

entries.title: A scout's warnings on NBA picks: the spots that still go wrong
entries.body: NBA picks now carry the scout's read: the situations a basketball person checks before trusting a pick, each measured on two full seasons against our own number. Six still go wrong often enough to say so, and the pick card says which, with what it measured: an under while a regular teammate sits out, an over after his minutes dropped, an over the night a regular returns, an under in a game the books expect to be high-scoring, a player whose games swing widely, and a player barely into his season. Situations the number already handles, or that measured as no problem at all (an over in a projected blowout, an over on the second night of a back-to-back), are not flagged. A warning moves no number; it is there so you can pass on a pick the record says goes wrong.

entries.title: NBA minutes stop being cut on back-to-backs and in blowouts more than they really are
entries.body: The NBA board's minutes numbers for back-to-backs and blowouts came from a written plan and had never been checked. Measured on two full seasons, a player who suits up on a back-to-back or a third game in four nights plays about his usual minutes, not the 4 to 8% fewer the board assumed. A 15-point favourite's starters lose about 5% in a likely blowout, not 14%, and the rotation players off the bench gain nothing, not the 20% the board gave them. The board now uses the measured numbers, leans a little more on a player's last five games, and trims a bench player's minutes 2%, because his recent stretch tends to overstate his next game. On a season it had never seen, minutes landed 3% closer and points, rebounds, assists and PRA 0.7 to 1.3% closer. The old numbers had leaned picks toward the under on busy nights and against heavy favourites.

entries.title: Basketball's corrections stop leaning to the over on rebounds, assists and threes
entries.body: Each week the NBA board re-learns how far to trust its own chances by replaying every game at a practice line: the player's recent average, rounded. Half the time that was a whole number, and a rebound or assist total lands exactly on a whole number about one time in five. Those pushes were left out, but the chance being corrected never allowed for them, so the correction learned that overs hit more often than they do. Checked on a full season it had never seen, it made rebound, assist and three-point overs about four points likelier than they hit, worse than no correction at all. The practice line is now always a half point, like the lines books post, and on the same season the corrected chances land within one to two points. It reaches the board with the next weekly refit.

entries.title: NBA points and threes read a player's shot volume, not his hot streak
entries.body: The NBA board projected points and threes from the last twenty games' makes. A three-point percentage over the hundred or so threes a starter takes in twenty games swings five points either way on luck alone, so a hot shooter's over looked like an edge the market had already discounted. Points and threes now come from his attempts a minute, which are his role, at his shooting percentages over his last sixty games pulled toward the league's. Points+rebounds, points+assists and PRA move only through their points. Measured on a full season of NBA games it had never seen, the projections landed closer for threes (1.7%), points (1.0%) and the three points combos (0.6 to 0.9%). Each pick's breakdown shows it as its own step, "Shooting, luck taken out".

entries.title: Six NBA ideas the play-by-play could not back
entries.body: Rebuilding who was on the floor every second of two full NBA seasons let us test ideas a box score cannot. Each was fitted on one season and judged on the next, and these did not improve the picks, so they are not on the board: a player's own record with and without an injured teammate (too noisy: it cost more accuracy than the bias it removed), the referees' crew, back-to-backs and home or away on a player's rate, his last five games over his last twenty, his share of the rebound chances, and the opponent's defence per possession instead of per game. The minutes a teammate's absence opens are still read, as before.

entries.title: Live scores keep moving on a night a game's feed fails
entries.body: The live pass reads each game's play-by-play four at a time. On a night one game's feed failed, the half-finished read could be cleaned up later on a thread that was just starting, and on the Python the site runs that thread waited on itself: the live scores and play rows sat still until the three-minute limit on each pass gave up on it, instead of moving every twelve seconds. Each batch of four now finishes and closes before its results are used, so nothing is left open to wait on. The same hang is what turned the code's own checks red on GitHub's Python 3.12 run.

entries.title: Long Shots show the players' faces again
entries.body: Since Long Shots became first-scorer picks (first touchdown for the NFL and college, first basket for the NBA), every card drew the player's initials: the first-scorer price list carries no photo, and the old board had taken its faces from the prop rows. Each board now gives those picks, and the lists of who scores first, the photo the same player's other props carry, or the sport's stored one; a name two photos claim is settled by the team or left as initials, never somebody else's face.

entries.title: Basketball's Most Likely picks are on the page again
entries.body: The NBA board built its Most Likely picks every day, and they were recorded and graded, but the page showed none of them. A check meant to hide a pick built on a broken number read a missing number as a claim of 0%, and NBA and NHL picks carry no such number, so every one was hidden. A missing number is now no claim, as the engine always read it, and the page lets through exactly the picks the engine posts. If a board ever has picks the page cannot show, the page now says so instead of saying the slate had nothing priced.

entries.title: The odds plan says where the month's credits went
entries.body: The plan's report now opens with the month so far: the credits used against the month's quota, how much of the month has gone, and how much of the month's spending the plan's own table puts in those days, so a month that opens with an NFL Sunday reads as on its pace and not as running away. A new day-by-day view lists what each day spent by sport, closing lines and slip checks, with the API's own count beside our ledger's. The day the plan renews is now read from the API's own count falling back to zero rather than estimated. How the credits are spent is unchanged.

entries.title: Most Likely learns from each market's record
entries.body: Most Likely's chances are corrected by their own graded record, and until now that record was read by where a pick came from and which side it took. A side can be honest as a whole while one market inside it claims too much: college receiving-yards unders hit about half the time where we said 70%. Now a market with enough graded picks is corrected on its own record, the rest are left as they were, and it is kept only when it predicts better on games it was not fitted on. A correction only ever lowers a chance and the tier follows it; no pick is taken off the board for its record alone.

entries.title: Fliff joins the books we compare
entries.body: Fliff's prices are now in the odds we compare, in the place of a second name for theScore Bet that the odds feed never answered to. Still ten books, so nothing else about the prices changes; a pick names Fliff when it has the best price.

entries.title: The weather desk is paused
entries.body: The prediction desk's weather calls claimed far more than they won: calls it rated at about 86% won about half the time. Until that is fixed it makes no calls, and its forecast board says it is paused. One cause is fixed already: the desk read each market's day from its closing time, which is in UTC, so an evening market could be priced against the next day's forecast; it now reads the day the market names. Out of sight, the desk keeps pricing and grading the calls it would have made, and it comes back only when those win about as often as they claim.

entries.title: The models' weekly refit reaches every sport again
entries.body: Once a week the models re-learn each sport from its whole history: how fast a player's form fades, each player's own correction, and how confident each market should be. That job ran every sport in one go, college first, and since 2 September it was stopped at its one-hour limit every week while still on MLB, so the NFL's deep refit last ran in late August. It now works in pieces, the NFL first, and picks up the next day where it stopped until every sport is done. A sport with no new games since its last refit, like MLB in the off-season, sits out. The nightly learning from each settled bet, the Most Likely board's own corrections and the losing-pattern blocks were checked the same day and were running.

entries.title: The college board builds through a busy morning
entries.body: From about 8 a.m. on 3 November the college board stopped rebuilding: every build died waiting to store last week's results, and the page kept showing the last good board. The holder was the pass that settles bets every five minutes: once the official NFL stats for Monday night arrived, each pass locked the results file and kept it locked for minutes at a time. It now lets go before it fetches anything. A build that still finds the file busy waits and tries again, and the college build no longer needs that refresh to publish — results it could not store are stored by the next build.

entries.title: College rosters open lighter
entries.body: The college rosters — every school's players, 41,878 of them, which the Rosters page and the player search read whole — now carry a detail only when it says something. The file the page reads went from 13.3 MB to 5.6 MB, so it opens quicker on a phone; nothing on the page changes.

entries.title: The Lab replays one sport at a time
entries.body: The Lab — the members' page that replays our models over history they never saw — stopped updating on 29 September. Its weekly run replayed every sport and published only at the end, and once the NBA and WNBA replays and five new NFL markets joined it, the run outgrew its hour and was stopped each night with nothing saved. It now replays one sport at a time and publishes each as it finishes, with that sport's own date on the page; a sport that runs long goes to the back of the next night's line instead of holding up the rest.

entries.title: The College Football Playoff bracket, from selection day
entries.body: From selection day (6 December) the college race page becomes the playoff itself: the twelve the committee names, seeded by its final ranking, every round — the first round on the higher seed’s campus, the quarterfinals and semifinals in the bowls, the title game — each score as it lands, and the champion. Free for everyone. For members: our line on every game still to play, and each team’s chance to reach each round and win it all, with every result already in kept.

entries.title: The NBA Cup's knockout bracket
entries.body: The NBA Cup page now draws the knockout rounds: each conference’s three group winners and its wild card, seeded; the quarterfinals at the higher seed; the semifinals at the better seed’s arena; the final in Indianapolis — each score as it lands and the champion. While group play runs it is the bracket if it ended today. Free for everyone; our line on each game still to play is for members, and the Cup’s chances now keep every knockout result already in.

entries.title: The facts around the games are free
entries.body: A free account now opens the standings, the rosters, the injury reports, each game’s weather, every team’s own page and the playoff races — the NFL’s, college football’s and the NBA Cup — as they stand: the seeds and the field if it ended today, and the standings. Our chances in the races, and every pick and price on the boards, stay with the plan. The Terms’ list of free features says so (§2, 3 November 2026).

entries.title: Today's free pick, as an alert, on the sign-up and as a picture
entries.body: The free Pick of the Day now travels. Turn on “Today’s pick, as an alert” at the top of the Pick of the Day page (or in Alerts) and your phone hears once a day when the pick goes up: the league and the pick’s record, never the pick itself on your lock screen. It is off until you turn it on. The sign-up screen and the plans now show today’s free pick with its price, whose fair it is and the Pick of the Day’s record, losses and all. And every pick on the page has a Share card button that draws it as a picture — the bet, the price at the book, the fair and the price’s chance, and once the game is graded, how it went. A graded pick also says Won or Lost on its card.

entries.title: The NFL playoff race
entries.body: The NFL now has a playoff race page, beside college football's and the NBA Cup. Free for everyone: the seven seeds in each conference if the season ended today (the four division leaders first, then the wild cards), the clubs in the hunt and how far back they are, and all eight divisions in tiebreaker order. For members: every club's chance to make the playoffs, win its division, take the 1 seed and win the Super Bowl, each game it has left at our price, and the week's games that swing the field most, with each club's chance either way. The rest of the season is played out 10,000 times on the same ratings as the Futures page.

entries.title: Each team's name is painted in its end zone
entries.body: On a live football game's Play-By-Play field, each team's name now lies inside its end zone, slanted with the field the way paint on the turf would be, with the tops of the letters toward the end line. It used to stand straight up while the end zone leaned, so its first and last letters hung off the colour. A long name is set smaller so it still fits.

entries.title: Prices come from the ten books most people bet
entries.body: The board now reads prices from DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM, Caesars, Fanatics, theScore Bet, Hard Rock and BetRivers, with Pinnacle as the sharp price our fair odds are measured against. Bally Bet, betPARX, Fliff, Wind Creek and the Novig and ProphetX exchanges are no longer quoted: the odds feed charges for every ten books asked for, so seventeen cost every refresh twice. The same credits now buy twice the updates.

entries.title: A payment that does not go through keeps the site one more day
entries.body: When a charge does not go through, the first after a free trial or a renewal, a member's access now stays on for one more day, 24 hours from the failed charge, and the account page, the email and the phone notice say until when. Update the card under Manage billing in that time and nothing pauses; if the payment has not gone through by then, access pauses until it does. The trial's day-before reminder says so too, and so does the Terms' §5.7.

entries.title: The Owner desk opens for the owner's own accounts alone
entries.body: The Owner desk (Who's on now, Accounts, money, reports, the notice to everybody) opened for the site's Qellys_Book account. It now opens for the accounts the owner lists on the server, by account rather than by address, since signing up does not prove an address, and for nobody else; every door to it on the server says the same, and the page shows its link only on the server's word. The site's problem alerts go to every listed account's phones, and a listed account cannot be suspended or deleted from the desk.

entries.title: The Terms say what a failed payment does
entries.body: Terms §5.7 said a member whose renewal failed would not be cut off on the first failure, which the site stopped doing on 12 October. It now says what happens: when a charge does not go through, the first after a free trial or a renewal, access to members' features pauses at once and we tell you; Stripe tries the card again, and updating it under Manage billing opens the site again as soon as a payment succeeds; if it is still unpaid when the retries run out, the subscription is cancelled and nothing more is charged. For an account made before 3 November it takes effect 30 days after we email the account about it, and the Terms say what applies until then. The same email tells every member about the free trial's two new rules and the Privacy Policy's two new parts.

entries.title: One free trial per person, not per account
entries.body: A new account, or the same address after deleting the old one, used to start the free trial again. From today the trial is one per person: an email address that has had one is not offered another, whatever the account, and a trial started with a card that has already had one is cancelled at once, with nothing charged, and the account page says why. To keep to it we hold a one-way fingerprint of a trial's address and card, made with a secret key so neither can be read back, for three years — after an account is deleted too, which is the point. The Terms (§5.3), the Privacy Policy (§2.3), the plans card, the checkout and the trial's FAQ all say so.

entries.title: The Owner desk can find any account and act on it
entries.body: The site's own account can now look up any account by email, username or number and see where it stands: how it signs in, its membership as its account page says it, whether it has had its free trial, its customer at Stripe, free access and suspension. From there it can give or end free access (a week to a year), sign the account out everywhere, suspend it (which signs it out and refuses every way back in, saying why) or lift that, reset a username that breaks the Terms, or delete the account after its email is typed. Suspend and delete wait while Stripe can still charge the account, and every step is written down where the desk shows it and in that member's Download my data. The Privacy Policy says all of it (§2.14).

entries.title: A charge that does not go through tells you, once, and the trial's last-day notice says what happens
entries.body: The day before a free trial turns into a charge (its third day), the email and the phone notice now say what happens if that charge does not go through: the trial is over and access pauses until the card is updated. And when a charge does fail — the first one after a trial, or a renewal — you hear once, on every phone signed in to your account and by email: access is paused, press Manage billing on your account page to update the card, and the site opens again as soon as the payment clears. The same failure is never told twice; a later one is told again.

entries.title: Cancelling a free trial ends its access at once, and there is one trial per account
entries.body: A trial cancelled on Stripe's page used to keep the members' pages until its three days were up. From today, cancelling a trial ends its access the moment we hear of it: nothing is charged, the account keeps the free side of the site, and it can never start another trial (checkout has always refused a second one, and the plans page stops offering it). The plans card, the checkout, the FAQ, the day-before reminder and the Live tab now say so before and during a trial, and so does the Terms' free-trial section (§5.3, dated 2 November 2026). A trial started before today keeps the rule it started under: access to the end of its three days.

entries.title: The site's own account always finds its desk, and Who's on now is part of it
entries.body: Signed in to the site's own account on the page itself (a password, a reset link, a passkey or a texted code), the page knew only the account's email until it was next loaded, so the owner's desk could be missing from Settings, and where it did show it sat at the very bottom, under Help. The page now asks who it is the moment a sign-in finishes; the desk heads that account's Settings and sits on its own profile beside Edit profile. Who's on now is no longer a page of its own: it is the desk's first card, still refreshed every ten seconds, and an old link to it opens the desk.

entries.title: Players' faces stay put after the site has been open a while
entries.body: A headshot that failed to load once — a dropped connection as the phone woke up or changed networks — gave up for good and left the helmet or initials in its place until that card happened to be drawn again, and every refresh of a board (every 30 seconds on a live night) drew each face from scratch, the helmet showing until the photo arrived, which on an iPhone could mean never. A face that has loaded now stays up across refreshes, and one that misses waits behind the helmet and is asked for again: a few times on its own, then whenever the page comes back to the screen or the connection comes back.

entries.title: The top of a game page is one wash of the two clubs' colours
entries.body: On the open Duo (and a phone with the app on its home screen), the top of a game page showed a black block over the sidebar, a bright band behind the logo and a darker one behind the score, and the bar behind the logo changed shade as you scrolled. The strip under the clock, the site's bar and the score bar now paint the same picture of the two teams' colours, so the top runs on as one; where the sidebar stands beside the page the score bar fits its column, so its back button shows.

entries.title: The owner's desk, and a notice bar the owner can put across the site
entries.body: The site's own account has a desk: who is on right now, accounts (new, signed in, came back), paying members, trials and the month's recurring revenue, today's picks by book beside the record, the site's health (crashes, how old each board is, the last update, when bets were last graded, odds credits left, disk), the community's day, and which optional features are switched on. Every number on it is a count or the business's own figure; nobody is named, and only that account can open it. From it the owner can put a short notice across the top of every page for an hour to a week (“Tonight's picks are late”, “New: …”), take it down, or let it run out; anybody can close it for themselves, and a new notice shows again. And what readers report — Feed posts and comments and, for the first time anywhere, game-chat messages — waits on the desk in one list with Hide, Keep it up and Restore: the words and the reasons, never who wrote or who reported them. When the site needs its owner — a board that has not rebuilt on a day its league plays, grading stopped, the disk filling, a failed update, odds credits running low — the desk says so at the top, and the phones signed in to that account hear it, once a day each.

entries.title: A live football game's Play-By-Play says what just happened
entries.body: The tab now leads with one card: the drive in progress (plays, yards, time), the down and where the ball is, and a field with each end zone in its club's colour under its name, the offense's logo on the line of scrimmage, the line to gain in gold, and only the last play drawn on it. A pass or a kick flies as an arc, a run or a return goes along the ground as an arrow, and what it came to is written at its end (“16-yd return”, “12-yd catch”, “Touchdown”). Under the field the same play reads as a sentence in our own words, with our win chance, the players in it and their game so far, and the down it was snapped on. The bar chart of the whole drive, a second “Ball on” strip and the separate Last play card are gone; the stadium picture stays, under the win chance, and the replay button flies the last play again.

entries.title: A first-touchdown pick counts on the record minutes after the game ends
entries.body: NFL first-touchdown Long Shots were graded off a public play-by-play file that arrives overnight, so a Sunday hit sat open into Tuesday and the Long Shots record did not move. They now grade off the game's own scoring plays within about five minutes of the final whistle, with the overnight file kept as the backstop for anything those cannot settle. On the Record page each kind of long shot now has its own line (first touchdowns, first baskets, and the home runs and anytime touchdowns before them), and every settled pick says which bet it was instead of “HR”.

entries.title: The Privacy Policy: Who's on now
entries.body: The site's owner now has a page, open to the site's own account and nobody else, that shows how many people are on the site right now and which of its pages they have open. Each open tab says which page it shows when that changes and about once a minute; the server keeps the latest for two and a half minutes, in memory, and never writes it down. Signed in, the page can show your username beside the page you have open: the Privacy Policy's new section 2.13 says exactly what, and Settings, Your data has a switch, "Show me in Who's on now", to stay off it and be counted without your name. An account made before 2 November is named only a week after we email it about the change, as the policy promises.

entries.title: Pages you are not looking at stop drawing in the background
entries.body: Since 25 October four pages, Most Likely, Long Shots, Trending and Players, were drawn on every load and every 30-second refresh, whichever page was open: a rename for accessibility left the list that keeps hidden pages waiting pointing at names no longer on the page. They wait again, and draw the moment you open them. Home now draws its own sections first and the Edge and Live pages' after, a few at a time, and the stadium pictures and their bands are worked out once rather than once per card. On a mid-range phone the time a first screen keeps the page from answering a tap fell by about two fifths on Home, a third on Live and half on the Record, and a refresh no longer redraws pages nobody is looking at.

entries.title: Every game page wears the two teams' colours
entries.body: A game's page now sits on its two teams' colours, the away side's from the left and the home side's from the right, deepening to dark further down, in every sport and in either theme. The score is big across the top with each team's crest, name and record and the ball beside whoever has it. Football draws the field under it: the yard lines, each end zone in its team's colour, the drive so far, the line of scrimmage, the line to gain in yellow and the down and distance over it. Under that is the score by quarter (by period in hockey). Football's page has four tabs: Stats (the odds, team stats with a bar for each side, both box scores and the game's details; a finished game leads with its scoring plays and leaders), Play-By-Play (Call it, the drive tracker, the field picture and the win chance while the game is on, then every drive, newest first), Standings (both teams' divisions) and Our picks. Scroll past the score and a compact bar keeps the score, the clock, the field and the tabs at the top. The TV delay, the second screen and Hide the score are under the ⋯ button by the score.

entries.title: Every page starts faster on a phone
entries.body: While the app started, five small checks of the page's size and position (where to scroll, how tall the header is, which fonts to load, whether the screen is folded) each made the browser lay out the whole page before it was built, and then do it again once it was. They now wait for the first frame, when the page has been laid out once anyway. On a mid-range phone the time the page can't answer a tap while it loads fell by about 40% on Home, 30% on Most Likely and 20% on the Live page.

entries.title: Opening on a page other than Home is quicker
entries.body: Opened straight onto Most Likely, the Record or any page but Home (from a link, or the app reopening where you left it), the site used to draw all of Home first, out of sight, before the page you were looking at. That page now draws first, and Home follows in small pieces that never hold up a tap; open Home before they finish and it draws the rest at once. On a mid-range phone the time the page can't answer a tap fell by about 15% on Most Likely and 30% on the Record.

entries.title: Same-game parlays are tracked, never staked; the rule from the first run is off
entries.body: The parlay study's second run read every league's games (1,821 of them; the first read only football's). It turned down the rule we added after the first: with it, the board's pairs made 9.0 units over 418 tickets, and without it 12.8 over 511. The same-game pairs it kept, the tightly linked ones, lost 15.9%, and it took away NFL Edge same-game pairs that had made 15.7%. What held in every run is the kind: same-game pairs lost 9.5% over 213 tickets and two-game pairs made 11.1% over 298 (10.9% for the Edge ones). So every same-game pair that makes sense posts again, one pick on each team included, and the Parlays page and the Record page grade it, but money now rides only on a two-game parlay whose two legs are both picks we stake, at half a unit. A same-game parlay is always tracked.

entries.title: Same-game parlays have to earn back the book's cut
entries.body: The first run of the parlay study on our own journal: football's Most Likely same-game pairs lost 11.7% over 86 tickets while its two-game pairs made 29.6% over 85. A book pays a same-game parlay about 9.5% under its two prices multiplied, and two heavy favourites in one game, joined only by the shared pace of the game, lift the chance both hit by 1 to 3%. So a same-game pair now posts only when the link between its legs lifts that chance by at least 10.5%, a quarterback and his own receiver, say. A pick on each team, which never carries more than the pace link, no longer posts. Edge parlays, which made 3.4% over 162 tickets (15.2% since mid-October), are unchanged. The study now also reads the NBA's and MLB's games, which its first run missed.

entries.title: Parlays: two legs from our own picks, with their own record
entries.body: Parlay Mode, the + Parlay button on every card and the do-it-yourself slip are gone, and so is High Confidence: the Most Likely list is ranked and does its job. Parlays is a button in the menu again, for the NFL, college, the NBA and MLB, in two sections. Edge parlays pair two Edge picks, ranked by what they return at the price; Most Likely parlays pair two of the likeliest picks, ranked by the chance both hit. Two picks from one game pair only when they belong together (teammates who rise together, or one pick on each team); the rest pair across games. Every ticket is journaled and graded off its two picks' own results, on the Record page apart from the singles, next to what pairing every graded day of our past picks the same way would have done. A two-leg parlay does what its legs do, about twice, so a ticket carries half a unit only when both its picks are ones we stake; the rest are tracked.

entries.title: College first touchdown counts the receivers again
entries.body: A college box score lists a receiver's catches but not his targets, and the first-touchdown board counted volume as carries plus targets, so receivers dropped off the list and the backs took every share: Duke's lead back read 52% to score the game's first touchdown, where the research's top bucket is 14%. A game with catches and no targets now reads its targets from the catches. On that game's shape the lead back reads 22% and the top receiver 18%, and no chance above 30% is ever a pick. The NBA's first-basket board now also says when the odds budget held tonight's prices, instead of saying they post later.

entries.title: Edge picks longer than +130 carry no stake
entries.body: Across every league, our Edge picks at +131 or longer hit 37.6% where the price itself said 41.1% and we said 42.9%, and the longer the price the wider the miss (+201 and up: 17.6% against 23.3%). That is the favourite-longshot bias: long prices pay less than their odds say. Those 293 picks lost 9.6 units; the picks at +100 to +130 made 23.8. Past +130 a pick still posts and is graded, on paper, and its card says Tracked · no stake.

entries.title: No per-market correction of our chances
entries.body: We measured pulling each market's chance toward the price by how that market had done, fitted on the season through Oct 15 and scored after it. It forecast no better than what runs now. In most leagues our Most Likely chances already forecast no better than the price itself; the NFL's Edge chances are the ones that beat it. Re-weighting the same number cannot fix that, so it was not built.

entries.title: The record leads with the picks we stake
entries.body: Edge picks are staked on the price ladder. Most Likely picks are now tracked for their hit rate instead of staked, until a league's Most Likely board proves it beats the price (the NBA's has). Across 7,542 graded picks, Most Likely won 60.8% of its bets and still lost 1.4%, because it pays −162 on average and 61.8% only breaks even. The record on the site now counts every graded pick at the stake that rule gave it on its day: 1,406 staked, +23.1 units, +3.2% ROI, with the price cap below. The record as placed stays on the Record page, and every number reruns from the public receipts (docs/STAKES.md).

entries.title: NBA Long Shots are first-basket picks
entries.body: Long Shots opens for the NBA. Who takes the first shot comes from both teams' tip records this season, and the team with the first shot scores first 71.9% of the time. Each player's chance comes from his share of his team's shots in the first three minutes. A pick needs a 10% edge at the best price, one a game, and is graded off the game's first made shot or free throw.

entries.title: First scorers before the prices
entries.body: Every first-touchdown and first-basket board now shows each game's likeliest first scorers by our numbers before the prices are in, with the price that would make each one a pick, and says why no price is on file yet.

entries.title: Receiving-yards unders come off the NFL and college boards
entries.body: On the graded Most Likely record, receiving-yards unders fell short of our chance in both halves of the season in both leagues: NFL 48% against 65%, then 48% against 53%; college 50% against 70%, then 50% against 62%. They're held back now, and the overs, which hold up, stay.

entries.title: Pages settle faster on a phone
entries.body: The first screen does far less work while it loads: on a mid-range phone, the time the page is busy and can’t answer a tap fell by about a third on the Most Likely page. A few style rules were making the browser re-check the whole page every time anything on it changed; they now ask only about what they style.

entries.title: College Long Shots are first-touchdown picks
entries.body: College football’s Long Shots now pick first-touchdown scorers the way the NFL’s do, on college’s own numbers: six seasons of college games for each team’s chance of scoring first, and each player’s share of his team’s carries, targets and touchdowns. A player is a pick only when our chance beats his price by 10% or more, one per game. Picks are graded off the box score once the game’s first scorer is known.

entries.title: Tight-end unders come off the NFL Most Likely board
entries.body: Our graded NFL board had a tight end’s under hitting 48% where we said 60%, over 100 picks and in both halves of the season. A tight end’s line is low and his catches come in bunches, so one busy afternoon beats it. Those unders now come off the board. A tight end’s over stays, and picks already posted are graded as usual.

entries.title: NFL Long Shots are first-touchdown picks
entries.body: The NFL’s Long Shots now pick first-touchdown scorers from our own numbers: each team’s chance of scoring first from the lines, and each player’s share of his team’s carries, targets and touchdowns. A player is a pick only when our chance beats his price by 10% or more, one per game, ranked by how far ours beats the price, never by the price itself. Under the picks, every priced player is ranked by our chance with the price beside it. College and NBA versions are next.

entries.title: NFL Most Likely asks more of a pick
entries.body: On the NFL Most Likely board, player props and game lines now need a 60% chance, up from 55%. Touchdowns keep 55%. Our picks between 55% and 60% won about as often as we said, but at those prices that wasn’t enough to beat the book’s cut. Unders that the game script works against also come off: a passing or receiving under on a team expected to trail, an under in a projected shootout, and three more our graded record caught. Picks already posted stay up and are graded as usual.

entries.title: Under pressure counts three seasons
entries.body: Clutch, reliability, comeback and choke now count this season and the two before it together, so a hot start can’t make a team 100% clutch off four close games. Each percentage shows the games behind it (“18 of 23”), and the record beside the team is the one those games add up to.

entries.title: Prices follow tonight’s games
entries.body: Sportsbook prices are now bought for the games being played tonight, league by league. A league’s next games get their prices on the day they’re played: Sunday’s NFL games on Sunday morning, a college Saturday on Saturday, a UFC card on fight day. Scores, schedules and live games update as always.

entries.title: A finished game reads like ESPN’s page
entries.body: A game that’s over no longer shows the live field or its last play. Its page opens on the final, the recap, the leaders and every scoring play, with the box score, every play and the team stats on the tabs. Basketball and hockey open a final on the shot chart. On the open Duo, the game chat’s bar sits at the bottom of the screen, beside the menu.

entries.title: An empty Most Likely board says why
entries.body: When a board has built tonight’s player props but their sportsbook prices haven’t been pulled yet, the Most Likely page now says so. It used to say the board fills in as the books post their menus, which read as though the sportsbooks hadn’t posted when they had.

entries.title: Every game a team has played has its own page
entries.body: Open a team and its Schedule tab: every game it has played opens a full game page, the kind ESPN draws — the final with both records, the game leaders, every scoring play with its drive (“7 plays, 66 yards, 3:23”) and the score after it, and tabs for the box score, every play and the team stats. The past meetings on the Versus tab open the same way, and tonight’s game still opens its board. The NFL, college football, the NBA, the WNBA, the NHL and MLB; UFC has fighters, not teams.

entries.title: No more blank cards on a game page
entries.body: Every game page drew three empty cards under the recap: the places kept for your bets on the game, the prop pace and the members’ split, each waiting until it had something to show. They stay out of sight until then now.

entries.title: The menu stays with you all the way down the page
entries.body: On an iPad, a computer or the open Duo, the menu beside the page now stays on screen however far you scroll. It used to ride up and off on the last screen of every page, where the footer pushed it. Slid away, its three dots stay with you too, and the page takes the room back.

entries.title: The book report card ranks the books
entries.body: The card on Line Shopping that measures which book prices sharpest had said “Not ranked yet” since it shipped in August: it read a price our line history has never written, so it measured nothing. It reads the history as written now — each book’s early prices against the closing consensus, one line and one game at a time, nothing after the start — over the last four weeks, and the card fills after the next daily run.

entries.title: A posted pick says the chance its tile shows
entries.body: When a posted pick’s chance drops under the bar, its note gives the new number. The books’ price could then lower that chance again, and the note kept the number from before — the board’s own self-check caught one pick saying one percentage in its note and another on its tile. The note now follows the tile.

entries.title: The Features page lists everything that shipped
entries.body: A month of features had never been written up there: weekly pick'em and private groups, karma and levels, the closing-line leaderboards, Call it, today's question and trivia, the player-of-the-game vote, watch parties and crew watch, Remind me, the Edge Report, Your data and the weekly limit. They are on it now, under a new Play along section and in Your account.

entries.title: No NBA Cup group has a leader before it plays
entries.body: The night before group play the Cup page tagged a leader in every group and a wild-card holder in each conference — at 0-0, on our ratings alone. The tags now wait for the first group game.

entries.title: The Pick of the Day is free
entries.body: One bet a day in every league is now free for everyone: a free account's Home opens the Pick of the Day page, every league's card side by side with the day's top pick first — the call, the bet, the price and the book, the sharp fair it was priced against, and each league's record. The rest of the board stays with membership, and so do the board's best bet on a day the pick sits out and the pick tracked live with its chance to cash.

entries.title: The day's top pick looks at every league
entries.body: Today's Top Pick is meant to be the strongest Pick of the Day across every league, and it never considered three of them. The NFL's board is dated by week, so its card never read as today's; hockey and the fight card, which have named picks since October, were not on its list. All seven leagues are ranked now.

entries.title: The Discord feed posts only a pick we would bet
entries.body: The picks channel checked a field the Pick of the Day never carried, so on a day the card said NO BET it could post the declined lean as the day's pick. It now posts only a card that says BET, and links to the free Pick of the Day page.

entries.title: The NBA Cup, group by group
entries.body: NBA → NBA Cup: the six groups with point differential and points scored, the wild card race, and how a tie is broken — head-to-head, then differential (an overtime game counts zero), then points. Members also get our chance for every team to advance, reach the final and win the Cup, and each group game left at our price and margin. Group play runs October 30 to November 27.

entries.title: The College Football Playoff race
entries.body: College football → Playoff race: the twelve-team bracket if it started today, from the poll (the committee's ranking from November 3) under the 2026 rules, and every conference's table. Members also get every contender's chance to make it, earn a bye, win its conference, win it all and win out, each game it has left at our price, and the games this week that swing the field. Our model plays the season out; the committee's final ranking is stood in for by a team's rating plus its strength of record, and the page says so.

entries.title: A day without a Pick of the Day still names a bet
entries.body: The Pick of the Day sits out roughly one day in three — its bar is stricter than the board's. On those days a member's card now says NO PICK TODAY and names the board's own strongest staked bet still to play, never the lean the day's bar turned down. How often the pick names one is on the card and the Record page: a pick on N of the last M slates, through yesterday.

entries.title: Three dots slide the sidebar away
entries.body: On a computer, an iPad on its side or an open foldable, three dots on the sidebar's right edge slide it away to the left and the page takes the whole width; tap them again, or drag the bar back, and it returns. On a touch screen you can also slide the bar away with your finger. Each device remembers how you left it.

entries.title: The phone's tab bar on the open Duo, tried for an evening
entries.body: For an evening the open iPhone Duo wore the phone app's tab bar, on its right edge on its side and at the bottom upright, with the menu as a sheet. Ethan liked the sidebar better, so the open Duo keeps the sidebar either way up, with the three dots to slide it away. Learned on the way, and written down so it is not tried blind: a web page cannot stand a bar under the Duo's clock either, because Safari 27.1 keeps web content out of that strip and paints it with the page's own colour. Only the App Store app can.

entries.title: The sidebar stays put
entries.body: On a tablet or an open foldable, the sidebar's list could be dragged sideways and pulled past its ends, and pulling it down refreshed the page. It now scrolls up and down only, and a pull or a swipe that starts in it stays in it.

entries.title: Your month, on the Karma tab
entries.body: The Karma tab now adds up your month: the live games you watched here, the days you earned karma, the karma, your pick'em record and how many of your calls were right, with a picture to share. From the 1st to the 7th it is the month just ended, and the card on the Live tab says so. If you said yes to keeping your activity, Monday's recap of your week now comes at the hour you usually look. And on a phone that gives the page a strip down its side, as the iPhone Duo does for apps built for it, the tab bar stands in that strip.

entries.title: The Terms and the Privacy Policy, changed, and a closing-line leaderboard
entries.body: Coming, each now in the Privacy Policy: a daily record of your own time here to time your alerts, kept only if you say yes (Settings, Your activity); the members' split, which counts the game-line legs of saved parlays into the share on each side a game's page shows unless you turn it off (Settings, Your data), and, for an account made by today, only from a week after we email it; and a closing-line leaderboard on My Bets, only for members who put themselves on it, ranked by price against the close and never by winnings. The Terms' changes of today apply to an older account 30 days after we email it; until then, the version of 26 October.

entries.title: The Privacy Policy and the Terms, brought up to date
entries.body: Both now describe everything added this month: pick'em groups and the rules for running one, what the morning and Monday alerts say, the notices about your own plan on your phone, quiet hours, limits and breaks, and what may not be posted here. A six-month or yearly plan now hears about three weeks before it renews, inside what state renewal laws ask.
